headline: High risk of shared-workspace data leakage and write conflicts; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are also material.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write configured working directories and Cline shares workspace files via VS Code, so content from one agent can be fed into the other through files. Cline also uses MCP and browser outputs, increasing the chance that AutoGen treats attacker-controlled content as instructions. The pathway exists in default-ish pair usage, though not via a dedicated shared channel.
conditions: IF AutoGen reads files that Cline wrote without provenance checks, injection is possible.
IF Cline writes browser-derived text into the shared workspace, AutoGen may parse it as instructions.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Disable file-based handoff between agents.
Add a provenance header to every inter-agent file.
Require manual review before AutoGen consumes Cline outputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystem content, and Cline shares state via filesystem while AutoGen uses configured working directories. That creates a default workspace leakage path for source code, browser screenshots, and application data. Neither profile shows a built-in isolation boundary strong enough to prevent accidental cross-reading.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory, files can flow between them.
IF sensitive application data is stored in the shared workspace, either agent can read it.
mitigations: Assign distinct directories per agent.
Mount sensitive data read-only for only one agent.
Remove secrets from shared workspaces before running.
Use a scrubbed handoff folder for any exchanged artifacts.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen and Cline both have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, and broad network egress; Cline additionally modifies git state. In a shared workspace, concurrent edits can overwrite files, corrupt builds, or race git operations. The profiles show no locking or coordination primitive, so conflict risk is high by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same workspace, concurrent writes can collide.
IF either agent commits or rewrites git state while the other edits files, repository corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Run agents in separate clones.
Serialize write phases with a human gate.
Disable git writes for one agent.
Use file locks on shared artifacts.
Snapshot the workspace before parallel runs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen can generate tool-using outputs that Cline may consume in the same workspace, and Cline has browser and MCP access plus approval-driven actions. If Cline treats AutoGen output as authoritative, a mistaken plan can cascade into real shell, browser, or MCP actions. The pair lacks a documented verification boundary, so the unsafe path is substantial.
conditions: IF Cline uses AutoGen-produced instructions without independent verification, errors can propagate to actions.
IF AutoGen emits incorrect commands that Cline executes after approval, downstream harm can occur.
mitigations: Require Cline to verify every AutoGen instruction against source material.
Insert a human approval step for all cross-agent actions.
Limit AutoGen to drafting only, not action planning.
Log and diff all proposed commands before execution.

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents handle model-provider API keys and user data, but the profiles do not specify residency, retention, or certification mismatches. The main compliance concern is that Cline’s browser screenshots and workspace files may expose regulated data to AutoGen through shared files. Because the mismatch is not explicit, this is a medium-risk documentation gap rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace, both agents may process it.
IF organizational policy forbids browser screenshots or code artifacts leaving one boundary, the pair may violate it.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared folders.
Review retention settings for both tools.
Use redacted test data for pair runs.
Document which agent may process which data class.
